items: How much money is it, and where does it go?

UNCTAD reports that foreign direct investment (FDI) flows worldwide rose 6% to $1.6 trillion in 2025, or 4% if money passing through major European financial centres is left out. Developing economies received $901 billion of the total: $644 billion to developing Asia, $188 billion to Latin America and the Caribbean, and about $70 billion to Africa. The countries UNCTAD classes as least developed received $43 billion, which UNCTAD gives as 2.7% of the world total; these countries are also counted in the regional figures. UNCTAD also reports that the top 20 host economies took more than 80% of global FDI in 2025.
Which countries does the money come from?

Two measures are used here. Stock means all investment built up over time; flow means new investment in a set period. By stock, a UN press release from 2003 says developed countries held almost nine-tenths of the world's outward FDI in 2002, and UNCTAD's 2026 report says about three-quarters now. By flow, UNCTAD reports that developed economies made up 72% of outflows in 2016 and nearly two-thirds over the past five years. UNCTAD also says developing Asia alone was one-third of outflows in 2025.
How much of the profit stays in the host country?

UNCTAD reports that foreign investments earned $1.5 trillion in 2011: nearly one-third stayed in the host economies and two-thirds went back to the investors. In developing countries the share staying was higher, about 40%. A 2025 paper by Parnreiter and colleagues, using IMF data for 2005-2022, puts the share of equity income sent home as dividends at 63.2% worldwide, and says counting only dividends understates the total. It finds six countries (US, Netherlands, Germany, Japan, France, UK) took 87.6% of net profit inflows, the US alone 41.2%. It finds 30 countries accounted for 84.0% of net profit outflows worldwide, and 44.1% of those outflows came from middle-income countries, including Russia (8.8%), Brazil (7.3%) and Nigeria (4.5%).
How much of it passes through tax havens?

UNCTAD's 2015 World Investment Report says some 30% of cross-border corporate investment is routed through offshore hubs, in a chart of investment stock labelled 2012. It estimates that developing countries lose about $100 billion a year in tax on investment directly linked to those hubs. Damgaard, Elkjaer and Johannesen wrote in an IMF magazine in 2019 that phantom investment, money passing through empty shell companies, had reached almost 40% of global FDI, up from about 30% less than a decade earlier. The UNCTAD and IMF magazine figures measure different things.

items: How much money is it, and who gives it?

The OECD's preliminary count puts official aid from the members and associates of its Development Assistance Committee at $174.3 billion in 2025. That is down 23.1% from 2024 after adjusting for prices and exchange rates, the largest annual drop the OECD has recorded. Two lines in its table make up about $157 billion of the total: grants from donors to recipients ($109.4 billion) and grants and capital payments to multilateral bodies ($47.8 billion). By amount, the largest national givers in 2025 were Germany ($29.1 billion), the United States ($29.0 billion), the UK ($17.2 billion), Japan ($16.2 billion) and France ($14.5 billion). EU institutions ($26.1 billion) are listed separately and are not part of the total. Twelve donors outside the committee reported another $13.3 billion.
How much of it comes back to the donor, and does it follow politics?

Eurodad reports that in 2018, 21% of bilateral and EU aid was reported as tied, meaning formally tied to buying from the donor, and 52% of untied contract awards went to suppliers in the donor's own country. The OECD's table shows 82.3% of donors' bilateral aid commitments untied in 2020, which leaves 17.7% tied or not fully untied (100 minus 82.3). The OECD also reports that in 2019-20, donor-country suppliers won 54% of contract value in the poorest countries covered by its untying recommendation, and 52% of value and 37% of contracts across all recipients. Kuziemko and Werker (2006), studying developing countries with US aid data for 1946-2001, find that a country's US aid rises 59% when it rotates onto the UN Security Council and returns to its earlier level soon after the term ends, within about two years. Dreher and colleagues (2018) find that Chinese grants committed to African countries in 2000-2012 rise the more closely a country votes with China at the UN; they find no statistically significant link for China's aid-like flows as a whole.
Who decides how the WHO's money is spent?

A BMJ Group press release from 2025 on a BMJ Global Health paper says around nine-tenths of WHO income is voluntary or extra-budgetary, and almost all of that is earmarked, meaning the donor sets what it pays for. The WHO's own page gives different figures: voluntary money is more than three-quarters of financing, and 87% of voluntary money was tightly earmarked in 2022-2023. The press release says the Gates Foundation was the WHO's second-biggest funder in recent years, after the US, at 9.5% of WHO revenue in 2010-2023. It reports 640 Gates grants to the WHO worth $5.5 billion in 2000-2024, almost 60% of that spent on polio and less than 1% on non-communicable diseases.
What is reported about the Gates Foundation and farming in Africa?

U.S. Right to Know reports that AGRA, a Kenya-based farm nonprofit, has raised over $1 billion, about two-thirds from the Gates Foundation. It reports that an evaluation by Mathematica, which AGRA says its programme partners selected, found AGRA did not meet its headline goal of raising incomes and food security for nine million small farmers. AGRA's written reply says it reached 10.1 million farmers, above its target of nine million, calls the mixed farmer results an expected outcome, quotes the finding that it fulfilled its role through improved policies and increased investment, and marks all eight recommendations accepted. U.S. Right to Know says the Gates Foundation did not respond to its questions. The African Centre for Biodiversity reported in 2015 that the foundation put over $85 million into a maize project using traits donated by Monsanto, and that for best yields farmers must buy new hybrid seed each year. EcoWatch, citing Bloomberg Businessweek, reported around 2016 that the project's director, Mark Edge, said it involves hybrid rather than genetically modified seed.

items: How much money is it?

World Bank tables show low- and middle-income countries' governments owed or guaranteed $2.097 trillion in long-term debt to private lenders at the end of 2024, more than the $1.463 trillion owed to official lenders. A further $2.611 trillion of long-term debt has no government guarantee and is not in those figures. The World Bank reports that flows from banks and other private creditors fell about 75% to $15 billion in 2024. It says bondholders and multilateral lenders supplied the vast majority of long-term inflows.
How much more do these countries pay to borrow?

UNCTAD reported in 2025 that since 2020 developing countries have borrowed at average rates two to four times those of the United States. That report said 3.4 billion people live in countries spending more on debt interest than on either health or education; UNCTAD's 2026 edition puts it at 3.7 billion, and says developing countries paid $995 billion in net interest on public debt in 2025. These people and interest counts cover all public debt, not only debt to private lenders.
Who gets paid?

Debt Justice counted external debt payments by 88 lower-income countries for 2020-2025, using World Bank data: 39% ($354 billion) to private lenders other than Chinese ones, 34% to multilateral lenders, 14% to other governments and 13% ($117 billion) to Chinese public and private lenders. The 2024 and 2025 amounts are scheduled payments on debts contracted by the end of 2023, not payments made. In a separate December 2025 article on bonds of 15 lower-income countries, Debt Justice lists BlackRock first among known bondholders. It estimates that BlackRock and its clients stand to make about $2.1 billion on $3.3 billion of bonds, an average of 64% more than if they had lent to the US government. The estimate assumes the bonds were held since they were issued, and the ownership data covers 23% of the bonds. The article prints no reply from BlackRock.

items: How much money is it?

World Bank tables show low- and middle-income countries' governments owed or guaranteed $475 billion in long-term debt to other governments at the end of 2024, compared with $987 billion to multilateral lenders and $2.097 trillion to private lenders. The World Bank reports that government-to-government lending flows fell to about $4.5 billion in 2024, the lowest since the global financial crisis, and "barely stayed positive" at under $2 billion for the poorest borrowers, those eligible for its IDA lending.
How much do borrowers pay back to governments?

Debt Justice counted external debt payments by 88 lower-income countries for 2020-2025 and found 13% ($117 billion) went to Chinese public and private lenders and 14% ($125 billion) to other governments. Multilateral lenders received 34% and other private lenders 39%. The 2024 and 2025 amounts are scheduled payments on debts contracted by the end of 2023, not payments made.
What does research show about the politics of this lending?

Dreher and colleagues (2018) studied Chinese development finance committed to 50 African countries from 2000 to 2012. They find China's aid-like money is driven mainly by foreign policy considerations, while its less generous, closer-to-commercial lending is better explained by economic interests. They also find that countries that do not recognise Taiwan receive more Chinese official finance.

figures.found: No opened page gives this split, for any total, year or counter. Pages checked: OECD 2026 ODA tables, World Bank IDR 2025, World Bank 'A Changing Landscape' 2021, Debt Justice 2025, Hudson Institute releases, Japan Ministry of Finance flows table. No total, year or counter can be named for it. Nearest real figures: World Bank table, long-term public debt end-2024, multilateral $987B, bilateral $475B, private $2,097B; the World Bank blog says multilateral lenders provided nearly half of long-term net financing in 2024. Neither gives 10%.

By debt owed the share is much larger: $475B of $8.937T total external debt stock (5.3%, my arithmetic).

figures.claim: Bilateral loans usually outnumber IMF and World Bank ones but are significantly smaller in size
figures.found: No opened page counts loans by number. On size: low- and middle-income governments owed $475B to bilateral and $987B to multilateral lenders at end-2024 (World Bank).

figures.claim: FDI mostly from developed countries: about 90% in 2002
figures.found: UN press release 2003: developed countries accounted for 'almost nine tenths of the world's outward stock in 2002'. This is accumulated stock, not yearly flow. ECB 2018 separately says almost 90% of outward FDI flows came from advanced economies until the Great Recession.

figures.claim: FDI from developed countries: 70% in 2016
figures.found: UNCTAD WIR 2017: developed economies were 72% of global FDI outflows in 2016 (74% in 2015). Yearly flow, so not comparable with the 2002 stock figure. Update: WIR 2026 says nearly two-thirds of outward flows over the past five years.

figures.claim: TNCs received about two-thirds (~65%) of what's generated abroad, almost twice what they reinvest in host countries
figures.found: UNCTAD WIR 2013: of $1.5T FDI income in 2011, 'nearly one third' retained in host economies and 'two thirds' repatriated; about 40% retained in developing countries, so 'almost twice' fits the world figure but not developing countries (about 1.5 times, my arithmetic). Parnreiter et al. 2025: 63.2% worldwide, 2005-2022 (IMF data). No page states ~65%.

figures.claim: Only 5 countries capture 80% of all net profit inflows
figures.found: Parnreiter et al. 2025 (IMF data, 2005-2022): six core countries capture 87.6% (US, Netherlands, Germany, Japan, France, UK). The likely original, Parnreiter et al. 2024 in Antipode 56:2343-2367, could not be opened (Wiley refused the fetch), so the 5/80% wording may be there, for a different period.

figures.claim: US alone 39.3% of net profit inflows
figures.found: Parnreiter et al. 2025: US 41.2% (2005-2022). 39.3% not found on any opened page; the Antipode 2024 paper could not be opened.

figures.claim: 30 countries account for 80% of the outflows
figures.found: Parnreiter et al. 2025: '30 countries account for 84.0 % of the losses world-wide' (2005-2022).

figures.claim: Middle-income countries the biggest net losers: Russia, Brazil, Nigeria
figures.found: Parnreiter et al. 2025: 'a large proportion of net profit outflows (44.1 % between 2005 and 2022)' from middle-income countries; Russia 8.8%, Brazil 7.3%, Nigeria 4.5% of global net outflows. The page says 'large proportion', not 'biggest'.

figures.claim: 30% of cross-border FDI routed through tax havens
figures.found: UNCTAD WIR 2015: 'Some 30 per cent of cross-border corporate investment is routed through offshore hubs' (chart labelled 2012). Disputed size: IMF F&D 2019 (Damgaard, Elkjaer, Johannesen) puts phantom FDI at almost 40% of global FDI, a different measure.

figures.claim: Foreign investors look for conditionality-privatization when deciding where to invest (footnote 2.23)
figures.found: No figure attached and no opened page confirms it; not traced further. The 'Claude AI estimates 20-40%' line is excluded as instructed.

figures.claim: In 2018, about 21% of rich-country bilateral aid was formally tied
figures.found: Eurodad: '21 per cent ... of bilateral and EU aid was reported as tied' (2018). OECD 2022 table for all sectors shows 77.2% untied in 2018, so 22.8% by subtraction. Update: OECD 82.3% untied in 2020, so 17.7%.

figures.claim: 52% of the remaining untied contracts still went to donor-country firms
figures.found: Eurodad: '52 per cent of all untied contract awards reported to the DAC' went to suppliers in the member's own country (2018). Update: OECD 2022, 54% by value and 37% by number in 2019-20 under the Recommendation.

figures.claim: When a country rotates onto the UN Security Council, its US aid rises 59%, then falls back when its term ends
figures.found: Kuziemko and Werker 2006: 'U.S. aid increases by 59 percent and its U.N. aid by 8 percent'; US aid returns to 'earlier level almost immediately upon completion of the term'. US aid data 1946-2001.

figures.claim: China's aid to African countries rises with how closely they vote with China at the UN
figures.found: Dreher et al. 2018 (2000-2012): 'An increase in voting similarity by 0.1 increases grant funding by 51 percent.' Holds for grants only: not statistically significant for ODA-like flows overall (p=0.123) or OOF-like flows (p=0.139).

figures.claim: About nine-tenths of the WHO's income, all of which is voluntary, is earmarked
figures.found: BMJ Group 2025: 'Around nine-tenths income comes from voluntary or extra-budgetary funding', almost all earmarked. WHO's own page: voluntary is 'more than three quarters', assessed dues under 20% to under one quarter, and about 87% of voluntary money was tightly earmarked in 2022-2023. Not all WHO income is voluntary.

figures.claim: The Gates Foundation is the second-largest WHO donor
figures.found: BMJ Group 2025: 'second biggest source of funding in recent years', 9.5% of revenue 2010-2023, after the US, ahead of Germany and the UK. Alliance magazine (June 2025) says WHO loses US funding in 2026 and China becomes the biggest state donor; no opened page gives a post-withdrawal ranking including Gates.

figures.claim: Giant foundations have budgets exceeding those of many international agencies
figures.found: No opened page states this comparison; not traced further.

figures.claim: Gates Foundation heavily promotes a high-tech, input-intensive model in African agriculture
figures.found: Only with attribution: U.S. Right to Know says AGRA raised over $1B, about two-thirds from Gates. African Centre for Biodiversity 2015 says Gates gave over $85M to WEMA and over $400M to AGRA. Mathematica found AGRA missed its headline goal for nine million farmers; AGRA calls that an expected outcome. No opened page has a Gates response.

figures.claim: Bayer/Monsanto, Corteva and Syngenta dominate this global market
figures.found: CBAN page: Bayer 23% of the seed market (citing Corporate Europe Observatory 2024), Corteva 19% (citing GRAIN and ETC Group 2025). No seed share given for Syngenta; about one quarter of agrochemicals.

figures.claim: Patented seeds often engineered to work only with own-brand herbicide
figures.found: No opened page says this for Africa. CBAN lists herbicide-tolerant GM crops approved in Canada: 22 of 33 Bayer, 6 Corteva, 3 Syngenta. Those figures are about Canada and do not show exclusivity.

figures.claim: Destroying seed-saving and an inescapable cycle of dependency for farmers
figures.found: Not shown in those words. African Centre for Biodiversity 2015 says hybrid maize cannot be replanted without significant yield loss, so farmers must buy each year, and that most maize is planted with re-saved seed (only 7% in Mozambique and 27% in Tanzania certified, 2010/11). That is one advocacy group's account. WEMA's director told EcoWatch it uses hybrid rather than GM seed.

figures.claim: Since 2020, developing countries have borrowed at rates two to four times higher than the US pays
figures.found: UNCTAD, 26 June 2025: 'two to four times higher than those for the United States'. The 2026 World of Debt page says rates are 'structurally higher' and gives no multiple.

figures.claim: 3.4 billion people live in countries that spend more on interest than on health or education
figures.found: UNCTAD 2025: 3.4 billion. Moved: A World of Debt 2026 gives 3.7 billion (data for 2025). https://unctad.org/publication/world-of-debt?lang=en

figures.claim: From 2020 to 2025, 39% of all external debt payments by 88 lower-income countries went to private lenders, three times what went to China
figures.found: Debt Justice, 11 Aug 2025: 39% ($354B) to commercial lenders excluding Chinese, 13% ($117B) to Chinese public and private lenders. 2024-25 are scheduled payments based on end-2023 contracts. 88 = 26 low-income, 51 lower-middle-income, 11 upper-middle-income small island states.

figures.claim: The largest known bondholder, BlackRock, stands to collect an average of 64% more than it lent
figures.found: Debt Justice, 22 Dec 2025: 'stands to gain an average of 64% more than it lent for itself and its clients'; $2.1B profit on $3,321M bonds across 15 countries, first among known bondholders. Assumes held since issue, profit measured against lending to the US government; data covers 23% of bond ownership. No BlackRock response on the page. Applies to BlackRock and its clients, not BlackRock alone.

figures.claim: Private lenders are mostly banks and investment funds in rich countries; debts enforced in rich countries' courts
figures.found: No figure attached and no opened page confirms it; not traced further.
